edge.title: The first meeting indoors
edge.setup: You've been chatting with someone from a dating app for a week. They're easy to talk to and suggest skipping the café: a friend's place is empty this evening, it's quieter, and there's no point paying for coffee. You are told to come alone, and you mention you'll wear your usual chain and ring.
edge.tell: The first meeting is private, at a place you did not choose, with no one who knows where you are.
move: Meet first in a busy public place you pick, in daylight or early evening.
Send a friend the person's name, photos and your live location before you go; agree a check-in time.
Do not wear or carry gold or other valuables to a first meeting, and do not go to an address you cannot leave on your own.
If anything feels wrong, leave first and explain later; 112 is the national emergency number.
edge.why: Every protection a stranger has to earn from you, such as witnesses, an exit, and someone who knows where you are, disappears when you move indoors on their terms. A stranger does not need to be dangerous for you to lose these; they only need you to agree to give them up before you know them.
edge.variants: Same shape: a 'quick look' at a flat with no one else around, a buyer who wants to meet at your home to inspect jewellery, a ride-share stranger who suggests a detour.

scenario.question: You have been chatting with someone from a dating app for a week. On Saturday evening they message: their friend's flat in a part of town you don't know is empty, it's quieter than a café, come alone. Nobody else knows you are meeting. What do you do?

choices.text: Say you'd rather meet first at a busy café you choose, send a friend their name, photos and your live location, and agree a check-in time.
Go to the flat. A week of good conversation is enough to know someone.
Go, but don't tell anyone, so it doesn't feel awkward if it goes well.
Agree to the flat, but ask them to pick you up so you don't have to find the address.

lens.name: Problems live at the seams
lens.one_line: When one system is split into several, the work that falls between the pieces is the work most likely to go undone.
lens.detail: Inside each unit, someone owns the job. At the boundary between units, everyone can reasonably say it belongs to the other side, and handovers are where files, calls and responsibility get dropped. Splitting a big organisation usually makes each piece easier to run and the joins harder to manage. So the question about any reorganisation is not whether the pieces are better, but who owns the cases that cross them.
elsewhere: A road dug up by one utility and left unrepaired because resurfacing belongs to another.
A complaint bounced between a building's developer, its association and the civic body.
A hospital bill disputed between the insurer and the TPA, each pointing at the other.
lens.test: If this goes wrong, which two offices will each say it belongs to the other?
lens.today: The Hindu reports that Bengaluru's police restructuring has left some divisions overburdened and others underutilised, and Deccan Herald says the top-heavy five-commissionerate split has exposed command overlaps; the chief minister is now discussing integrating them. Five commissionerates means more boundaries, and complaints that cross them, such as a phone stolen in one area and traced to another, are where delays tend to show up. Until the lines settle, file at the nearest station and keep the acknowledgement and FIR number.

moved.what: BMRCL has sought safety clearance to begin trial runs on the Pink Line's underground stretch and is aiming for a May 2027 opening, Moneycontrol and Swarajya report. A separate News18 report says trial runs have begun on the Blue Line.
moved.so_what: Trial runs come before safety approval, and opening dates often slip. If you are choosing a flat or signing a lease because a Pink Line or Blue Line station is coming, plan around today's commute, not the target date.

moved.what: The Jakkur railway overbridge has opened after a 15-year wait and is expected to ease traffic in North Bengaluru, Asianet Newsable reports.
moved.so_what: If you drive through Jakkur towards Yelahanka or the airport side, try the overbridge once at your usual hour this week and time it against your old route. Expect traffic to shift onto it, and onto the roads leading to it.

moved.what: Gold is heading for its worst week since March, with bets on a US Federal Reserve rate hike and forced selling weighing on prices, FXStreet reports.
moved.so_what: Indian gold prices broadly follow the international price. If you are buying for the wedding season, one weak week is not a signal to rush. Splitting the purchase across a few dates evens out the swings, and whenever you buy, check for the BIS hallmark and HUID on the piece and the bill.

moved.what: Karnataka has launched a five-year plan to tackle antibiotic resistance, The Times of India reports.
moved.so_what: The easiest part of that plan is in your hands. Do not ask a pharmacist for antibiotics for a cold or viral fever, because they do not work on viruses. When a doctor does prescribe them, finish the full course.

carry_over.prompt: On a crowded metro coach, someone has held a phone still at hip height for two stops, lens toward you, thumb off the screen, and you are not yet sure; what is the sign that you are being filmed?
carry_over.answer: A phone held still with the lens toward you and no one touching the screen.
